title: N-Queens II
description:
# N-Queens II

The **n-queens** puzzle asks you to place `n` queens on an `n x n` chessboard so that no two queens attack each other. Queens attack along rows, columns, and both diagonal directions.

Return the number of valid placements rather than the boards. One set of occupied cells is one placement; queens have no separate identities.

For `n = 4`, the two valid placements have row patterns `.Q.. / ...Q / Q... / ..Q.` and `..Q. / Q... / ...Q / .Q..`.

## Example 1:

**Input:** n = 4
**Output:** 2
**Explanation:** There are two distinct ways to place four queens without attacks.

## Example 2:

**Input:** n = 1
**Output:** 1
**Explanation:** A single queen on a one-cell board is valid.

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= n <= 9`

tests.description: minimum board has one valid placement
two queens cannot be placed safely
three queens also has no solution
odd board with more than one symmetry class
larger even board catches diagonal-index mistakes
mid-sized odd board checks full counting
upper bound for the official constraint

solutions.name: Boolean Arrays Backtracking
solutions.description:
## Approach

Place one queen per row. Three boolean arrays record occupied columns, main diagonals, and anti-diagonals. When a candidate square is free in all three arrays, mark it, recurse to the next row, and unmark it while backtracking.

## Key Insight

A board position is unsafe exactly when its column, `row - col`, or `row + col` has already been used. Counting complete row placements avoids building any board strings.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n!)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Bitmask Available-Position DFS
solutions.description:
## Approach

Represent occupied columns and the two diagonal families as bitmasks. At each row, combine those masks to get every safe column bit, repeatedly take the lowest available bit, and shift diagonal masks for the next row.

## Key Insight

The set of safe columns for a row is `fullMask & ~(columns | diagonals | antiDiagonals)`. Bit extraction removes one legal choice in constant time and keeps the search state compact.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n!)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: First-Row Symmetry Pruning
solutions.description:
## Approach

The chessboard is symmetric across the vertical center line. Put the first queen only in the left half of row zero and double those counts. For odd `n`, search the middle column once because it mirrors to itself.

## Key Insight

Symmetry only changes the first decision. After that decision, the same bitmask DFS counts the remaining rows without accidentally double-counting mirrored boards.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n!)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Permutation Diagonal Scanner
solutions.description:
## Approach

Treat a partial board as a permutation: `queenColumn[row]` stores which column was chosen for that row, and `usedColumns` prevents duplicate columns. Before accepting a new column, scan earlier rows to reject diagonal conflicts.

## Key Insight

Choosing one column per row automatically satisfies row and column constraints. This route keeps the diagonal rule visible and is useful before introducing diagonal arrays or bitmasks.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n! * n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)
